bib.title: Statistical Rethinking, Chapter 4: Linear Models
bib.venue: book chapter (Statistical Rethinking, first-edition style, map/rethinking package)

question: How does one build, fit and interpret a Gaussian linear regression as a Bayesian model with priors, a likelihood and posterior sampling?
contributions: Why Gaussians arise (addition, small multiplication, log-multiplication) and two justifications for using them
A model-definition language: likelihood, linear model, priors
Gaussian height model by grid approximation and quadratic approximation (map)
Linear regression with a predictor, centring, posterior line samples, mu and prediction intervals via link and sim

limits: Chapter frames linear regression as a descriptive 'geocentric' model; polynomial regression is called generally a bad idea (p110).
Quadratic approximation is poor for sigma (long right tail) unless log(sigma) is used (p86, p91).
Zero-centred Normal(0,10) prior on beta is acknowledged as silly for height vs weight, harmless only because of much data (p95).
Uses the old rethinking::map interface (later renamed quap); code dated.
Intervals are conditional on the model: even a bad model gives tight intervals (p107).
practices: Describe every model as outcome likelihood, linear model, and priors for every parameter (p77).
Plot priors and simulate heights from the prior before fitting (p82-83).
Check sensitivity by changing priors and refitting; there is no uniquely correct prior (p95).
Report 89% intervals rather than conventional 95% so readers do not read them as significance tests (p88).
Centre predictors to make the intercept interpretable and remove a-b correlation (p99-100).
Standardise predictors, especially for polynomials, to avoid numerical glitches (p111).
Plot posterior inference against data rather than reading tables alone (p97-100).
Propagate parameter uncertainty by computing any quantity for each posterior sample (link/sim recipe, p106-108).
Keep parameter uncertainty (mu interval) distinct from sampling uncertainty (prediction interval) (p109).
Estimate log(sigma) when the quadratic approximation for sigma is poor (p91).
Do not choose the Gaussian likelihood by eyeballing the outcome histogram (p81).

terms.definition: make the parameter for the mean of a Gaussian distribution, µ, into a linear function of the predictor variable and other, new parameters that we invent
maximum a posteriori estimate; the posterior's peak, around which the quadratic approximation is built
Gaussian approximation of the posterior at its peak; multivariate Gaussian described by means and a variance-covariance matrix
subtracting the mean of a variable from each value
first center the variable and then divide it by its standard deviation
each value has the same probability function, independent of the other values, using the same parameters; an epistemological not ontological assumption
highest posterior density interval computed from posterior samples
link computes mu for each posterior sample and case; sim simulates observed heights incl. sigma

code.snippet:
sample_mu <- rnorm( 1e4 , 178 , 20 )
sample_sigma <- runif( 1e4 , 0 , 50 )
prior_h <- rnorm( 1e4 , sample_mu , sample_sigma )

m4.3 <- map(
alist(
height ~ dnorm( mu , sigma ) ,
mu <- a + b*weight ,
a ~ dnorm( 156 , 100 ) ,
b ~ dnorm( 0 , 10 ) ,
sigma ~ dunif( 0 , 50 )
) ,
data=d2 )

post <- extract.samples(m4.3)
mu.link <- function(weight) post$a + post$b*weight
